summary: A proposal from John Davidson, Will Crowther, John McConnell and Jon Postel describing an echoing strategy for terminals connected over satellite links. Because each character must travel to the server and back, echo can feel sluggish, with delays of nearly half a second or more. The note outlines why this is a problem and how echoing might be organized to reduce it. It builds on RFC 346.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposal aims to make remote terminal typing feel more responsive over satellite links. The server controls when input is echoed, while the user's Telnet displays characters locally.

subtitle: A proposal to reduce the effect of satellite delay by echoing terminal input at the user's site.

tldr.problem: A character sent over a satellite link may take nearly half a second to reach the user again, making interactive typing feel sluggish.
tldr.mechanism: Remote Controlled Echoing lets the server define break behavior while the user's Telnet performs echoing locally and switches among echo, output and discard paths.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes an optional Telnet addition and says simulation and an experimental implementation should come next.

sections.title: Why Satellite Echo Feels Slow
sections.content:
For an interactive terminal, a character's round trip over the network adds to the server's echo delay. The RFC estimates that over a single satellite link, key-to-display latency is nearly half a second even if the server echoes instantly; routes through the surface network add more delay.

The proposal describes an optional addition to existing User Telnet programs and requires a cooperating server process. It aims to remove the delay associated with simple echoing.
sections.plainLanguage: When the server must echo each typed character across a satellite link, the user waits for the round trip. This proposal tries to show typed characters locally while preserving the server's control.

sections.title: Wakeup and Break Characters
sections.content:
In the standard approach described here, a server's Terminal Handler echoes characters and buffers user input. A user process can name wakeup characters that cause it to receive input and break characters that stop echoing while the process prepares a response. Echoing resumes after the response completes.

The process can also ask that input not be echoed, which is useful for hidden input. For example, a break character may signal that a password should not be displayed.
sections.plainLanguage: A wakeup character tells the remote program to process input. A break character pauses echoing so the program's response does not mix with the next command.

sections.title: Remote Controlled Echoing
sections.content:
With Remote Controlled Echoing (RCE), the server controls the echo rules, but the User Telnet in the TIP performs the echoing. Typed characters go into input and transmission buffers. Server commands control whether characters are discarded, echoed to the terminal, or output from the server is shown.

The proposed commands include Use RCE, Set Break Action, Set Break Classes, Move to Break (MTB) and Delete to Break (DTB). MTB moves input through the print path up to a break; DTB discards input through a break, which can hide a password. The server and user must cooperate, and the server answers a request to use RCE with YES or NO.
sections.plainLanguage: The server tells the user's Telnet when to show typed characters, hide them or display the server's reply. The local Telnet can show input without waiting for each character to travel to the server and back.

sections.title: Trade-Offs and Open Questions
sections.content:
The proposal says transmission delay becomes noticeable at break interactions, where the server processes a command. Users who type ahead may overlap transmission and processing with earlier output. The document discusses unsolicited server output and lists unresolved questions about buffers, break classes, transmission timing and formatting characters.

The RFC does not recommend discarding current Telnet. RCE is optional and should not be used for half-duplex devices that echo themselves. The authors say the next steps are simulations and an experimental Telnet version.
sections.plainLanguage: RCE may reduce delays between ordinary keystrokes, but processing delays can still appear at command breaks. The proposal keeps existing Telnet available and leaves several details for further work.
